c1.claim: Harmful runs fell from 66.7% blind to 5.6% with the Ekbasis guard (K-H1 passed).

c2.claim: K-H2 failed: the Ekbasis guard was not shown non-inferior to the same guard with Sonnet as forecaster.

c3.claim: Asking before every command also avoided all harm with this simulated user, so what the forecaster adds here is asking a third as often, not more safety than asking every time.

c4.claim: All 3 harms under a guard came from a gap in the simulated user; the verdicts count them as harm.

c5.claim: The Ekbasis guard measured here is Ekbasis plus code checks plus a hand-written safer-way catalog, on task families chosen where Ekbasis was already strong; it is not Ekbasis alone.

c6.claim: With Sonnet as the agent, harmful runs went from 33.3% to 0% with the Ekbasis guard (secondary, one seed).

c7.claim: The Ekbasis latency figures are for a 4-bit MLX build on one shared Mac and say nothing about latency on GPU.

c8.claim: The Ekbasis guard has no per-call API cost and keeps the cluster state on the local network; the hardware that serves it is not priced.

c9.claim: No evaluation item was found in the published training lineage; withheld rows and the base model's pretraining could not be checked.

c10.claim: Task success rose from 30.6% to 83.3% with the Ekbasis guard; success requires the goal met and no harm, so it rises partly because harm fell, and asking every time reached the same 83.3%.

x1.claim: Ekbasis was shown to be as good a forecaster as Sonnet (non-inferior).

x2.claim: The Ekbasis guard made the agent safer than asking the user before every command.

x3.claim: The study shows the Ekbasis guard answers in about one second per check.

x4.claim: The pre-registered go/no-go rule of Phase 0 approved running Phase 1.
